title: Farm Fires Fall Sharply, but Delhi's Air Turns 'Very Poor' at AQI 324
excerpt: Delhi posted its worst air since February even as NASA counted fewer Punjab and Haryana farm fires than last year — a reminder that local emissions and calm winter weather, not stubble alone, now set the capital's AQI.
body:
• Delhi recorded its first 'very poor' air of the season on Monday, November 2: the Central Pollution Control Board's 24-hour average AQI reached 324, the highest since February 4, with Jahangirpuri at 436, Rohini at 415 and Punjabi Bagh at 413 — all in the 'severe' band above 400.
  • Satellite counts show farm fires falling, not rising: NASA recorded 1,394 fires in Punjab and Haryana from October 1 to November 1, down from 1,861 in the same period last year — though officials caution that burning has shifted to evening hours satellites miss.
  • The Commission for Air Quality Management imposed GRAP Stage II across Delhi-NCR on November 2, and the Air Quality Early Warning System forecasts 'very poor' air until November 5.
  • If you are in Delhi-NCR this week: prolonged exposure above AQI 300 carries health risks, especially for children, older people and those with respiratory illness — doctors advise limiting outdoor activity in the morning and evening peaks and wearing a protective mask outdoors.

Delhi's air crossed into the 'very poor' category for the first time this season on Monday, November 2 — and it did so in a year when the usual suspect, stubble burning, is at its weakest in years. According to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), Delhi's AQI stood at 312 at 9 a.m. on Monday and the 24-hour average reached 324 by the 4 p.m. bulletin, the highest since February 4, when it stood at 339, Jagran reported. On the CPCB scale, 301 to 400 is 'very poor' and 401 to 500 is 'severe'. Three stations crossed into severe at 4 p.m. — Jahangirpuri at 436, Rohini at 415 and Punjabi Bagh at 413 — while 37 of the 58 reporting stations recorded 'very poor' air. India Today's coverage put the city average at 331 by Tuesday morning, with several areas above 400.

The numbers behind the apparent paradox

The deterioration was fast. Delhi's 24-hour average AQI was 261 ('poor') on Sunday, up from 117 ('moderate') a day earlier; on Friday it had been 60 ('satisfactory') after heavy rain washed pollutants out of the air, according to CPCB data reported by Zee News. PM2.5 — the fine particles that travel deep into the lungs — was the dominant pollutant at 51 of the 58 stations reporting on Monday morning.

Farm fires, meanwhile, are down on the satellite record. NASA data recorded 1,394 farm fires across Punjab and Haryana between October 1 and November 1 — 1,249 in Punjab and 145 in Haryana, with 171 detected on November 1 alone — against 1,861 in the corresponding period last year. A longer view from a Chapter One analysis of official data shows Punjab's fire count falling from 83,002 in 2020 to 5,114 in 2025 on Punjab Pollution Control Board figures, and the CPCB itself, replying to an RTI request, put stubble's average share of Delhi's PM2.5 between October and December at 13 per cent in 2020 and just 3.5 per cent in 2025.

Two cautions on the fire count

The satellite numbers come with an honest caveat, reported by both Zee News and the Chapter One analysis: burning has shifted later in the day. Meteosat data showed around 98 per cent of fire heat detected in 2025 occurred after 3 p.m., after the roughly 1:30 p.m. observation window of the satellites used for the headline counts, so the true number of fires in both years is likely higher than recorded. Even allowing for that, the direction of travel is not in dispute — and neither is the conclusion it forces: with stubble's average share in the low single digits, most of what Delhi breathed this week was generated in and around the city itself, then trapped there.

What is driving the air now

The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM), in its November 2 order imposing Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) across Delhi-NCR with immediate effect, cited unfavourable meteorological conditions, with forecasts from the India Meteorological Department and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology indicating air would stay in the 'very poor' category. Meteorologist Navdeep Dahiya, quoted by Zee News, pointed to calm conditions with winds from the north-west, meaning emissions persist in the atmosphere for longer. Local sources — vehicles, dust, construction and the city's own emissions — do the rest once the winter lid settles. Noida, in the wider NCR, recorded an overall AQI of 305 on Monday.

What to do this week

The Air Quality Early Warning System for Delhi forecasts 'very poor' air until November 5, with marginal improvement to 'poor' over the following six days — and Diwali, when firecrackers add to the load, is still ahead. Medical experts cited by Jagran warn that prolonged exposure at AQI levels above 300 poses health risks, particularly for children, the elderly and people with respiratory conditions; the advice is to limit outdoor activity, especially during the morning and evening hours when pollution peaks, and to wear a protective mask when travelling outdoors. You can follow station-level readings on the live CPCB air-quality tracker. Separately on Monday, the Delhi High Court refused an immediate stay on the bar on non-BS-VI outstation vehicles entering the city, with a hearing scheduled for November 27.

nri_angle: For diaspora families with parents and relatives in Delhi-NCR, the useful fact is that this week's severe air is driven mainly by local emissions trapped by calm winter weather, not by a stubble surge — and GRAP Stage II curbs plus 'very poor' forecasts run through November 5.
author: Diaspora Desk
